nameStory: The Turf Running Spider gets its name from its lightning-fast sprinting abilities and preference for low-growing vegetation like grass and ground cover. Unlike web-building spiders that wait patiently, this athletic hunter actively runs across turf and foliage to chase down prey. The 'running' part of its name becomes obvious when you watch one dart across a lawn or garden bed with surprising speed.
description: The Turf Running Spider is a small, active hunter that belongs to the running crab spider family. These compact spiders have a flattened, crab-like body shape that allows them to move sideways and backwards with ease. They're typically small enough to sit comfortably on a dime, with females being slightly larger than males. Rather than spinning webs to catch prey, they actively hunt during the day, sprinting across vegetation to ambush insects.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Runs sideways and backwards like a crab when disturbed, with quick, jerky movements across leaves and stems rather than dropping on silk like many spiders

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Flattened, crab-like body that feels firm to the touch, with the front two pairs of legs noticeably longer and held out to the sides

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No web structure - only leaves behind thin silk draglines that feel like barely-there threads when brushed against

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small enough to rest on a dime with legs extended, females slightly more robust with a fuller abdomen

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Variable coloration often matching their plant host, typically in earth tones with subtle patterns that can feel slightly fuzzy under magnification

habitat: Look for Turf Running Spiders on low vegetation, grass, shrubs, and in gardens throughout New England. They're particularly fond of fruit trees and ornamental plants where they hunt for aphids and small insects. You'll often find them sunning themselves on leaves during warm days, especially in areas with mixed vegetation rather than dense forests.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, often seen hunting on emerging foliage and early garden plants. Males begin their distinctive courtship tapping behavior on females during late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most easily observed hunting during daylight hours. Mating occurs frequently, with interesting plug-removal behaviors between multiple males and females.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall as they take advantage of remaining insect prey. Egg-laying likely occurs during this period before winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Inactive and hidden under bark, leaf litter, or other protected locations. Not observable during cold months in New England.

funFact: Male Turf Running Spiders are spider gentlemen with a twist - they can actually remove the mating plugs left by previous males, essentially giving themselves a second chance at romance with females who have already mated!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other running crab spiders in the same genus, but the Turf Running Spider's preference for low vegetation and ground-level hunting helps distinguish it from tree-dwelling relatives. Remember: if it's running on turf and low plants rather than high in trees, you've likely found the right species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'crab spiders,' running crab spiders are actually in a different family from the true crab spiders (Thomisidae) that sit motionless on flowers. The 'crab' name refers only to their sideways movement and leg positioning, which can confuse beginners trying to identify spider families.
compareHints: The Turf Running Spider differs from its Philodromus relatives primarily in habitat preference - while the Metallic Crab Spider tends toward trees and the White-striped Running Crab Spider prefers taller shrubs, the Turf Running Spider sticks to low vegetation and ground cover. It's also one of the most common in agricultural areas, particularly orchards, where it provides natural pest control by hunting aphids and other crop pests.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin the White-striped Running Crab Spider which has obvious white stripes, the metallic crab spider males are uniformly shiny without stripes.

The white-striped running crab spider is distinguished from its relatives by those prominent longitudinal white stripes - most other Philodromus species in New England have more subtle markings or different color patterns.

Compared to other Philodromus species in New England, the Resplendent Running Crab Spider stands out for its particularly brilliant metallic appearance - more lustrous than the Metallic Crab Spider and lacking the white stripes of the White-striped Running Crab Spider.

Among its Philodromus relatives in New England, the male's distinctive shiny black coloration with white edges makes it relatively easy to distinguish from the more uniformly colored Metallic Crab Spider or the striped patterns of the White-striped Running Crab Spider.
The Minute Running Crab Spider is significantly smaller than its relatives like the Metallic Crab Spider or White-striped Running Crab Spider, which are much more commonly encountered.
Philodromus exilis is notably more slender than the Metallic Crab Spider or White-striped Running Crab Spider, lacking the metallic sheen or distinct striping of those relatives.
